small_guidance:
- The two-pass partials approach adds an extra global round-trip for the row sums. Eliminate the partials buffer by using a single-pass GEMM kernel where each program handles a full row tile (BLOCK_N = N or a persistent K-loop over all N tiles) and accumulates the sigmoid-sum directly into a per-row atomic_add on `out`. With M=128 and N=32768, one program per (M_tile, N_tile) doing `tl.atomic_add(out + offs_m, row_sum, mask=m_mask)` removes the second kernel.
- Add larger-K configs (BLOCK_K=128) and BLOCK_M=16 / BLOCK_M=32 configs since M=128 is small — using BLOCK_M=128 gives only 1 program along M, starving the GPU of parallelism. Favor BLOCK_M=16 or 32 with BLOCK_N=256, num_warps=8, num_stages=4 to get 8-16x more N-tile parallelism per row tile.
- Add a GROUP_M swizzle (group_m=8) on the (pid_m, pid_n) mapping for better L2 reuse of the weight tiles across row groups.
large_guidance:
- Restructure as a split-K-style single-kernel design: grid is (cdiv(M, BLOCK_M), cdiv(N, BLOCK_N)). Each program computes its (BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N) GEMM tile, adds bias, applies sigmoid, reduces along N within the tile to a (BLOCK_M,) vector, and `tl.atomic_add`s into `out[offs_m]`. This fuses everything into one kernel, removes the partials tensor and the second reduction launch, and keeps all intermediate sigmoid values in registers.
- Since K=N=32768 is huge, consider a persistent kernel: launch only ~128 SMs worth of programs, each iterating over a list of (m_tile, n_tile) work items, so weight columns loaded by one tile can be reused for the next row of the same n-tile range via L2. With M=128 the M dimension is tiny — one program per (row_tile, n_tile) with BLOCK_M=32, BLOCK_N=128 gives ~4×256=1024 tiles which maps well to persistent scheduling.
- Store weight as (K, N) contiguous (already done) and prefer BLOCK_K=64 with num_stages=4 to overlap the long K loop; the kernel is compute-bound on tl.dot for these sizes, so maximizing MAC throughput with proper pipelining matters more than memory tricks.
